briefing.headline: The simulation predicts the three-fixed-days mandate would nearly triple departures over the next 12 months, from about 364 to about 1,038 of 5,000 employees (+182%, roughly 670 extra leavers); read this as a strong warning signal rather than a precise forecast.
briefing.most_at_risk: Employees with long commutes react worst (+250% leaving vs +133% for short commutes), followed by caregivers (+220% vs +165%) and mid-level staff (+197%), because fixed office days cost them hours of travel and break childcare and eldercare arrangements they built around flexibility.
risks: Mid-level and long-tenured people may leave, not just new hires: several modelled managers and directors with 11 to 15 years of service say they will start looking, and competitors in the field still offer flexibility.

Badge tracking reviewed with managers is read as distrust even by people who plan to comply, so the average reaction is strongly negative (-1.29 on a -2 to +2 scale) and morale among those who stay is likely to suffer.

Requiring VP approval for exceptions discourages caregivers and long-commute staff from asking ('I'm not counting on one'), so they look for other jobs quietly instead of raising the issue, and attrition may surface late and with little warning.
design_changes: Let teams choose their own anchor days, or allow a weekly or monthly office target, instead of three company-set days, so people can fit office time around school runs, care duties and long commutes.
Drop individual badge-swipe reviews, or report only team-level attendance, and explain plainly what in-office time is meant to achieve for the work.

Let direct managers approve exceptions using published criteria (for example caregiving or commutes over a set length), phase the change in over a longer period than 90 days, and test these variants in a re-run of the simulation before announcing.
briefing.confidence: medium, because the direction is consistent across every group and every modelled voice, but the figures rest on only 48 modelled voices (about two per group), so the 1,038 figure and the gaps between groups should not be quoted as forecasts.

subgroup_checks.claim: Bigger rise for mid and senior managers
